overview.text: The Three Holy Hierarchs icon joins Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom. Their common feast emphasizes concord in teaching rather than rivalry among their admirers.
overview.reason: Necessary concise account of the named copyrighted publication; full-text reproduction permission has not been established. Traditional events and published interpretations remain attributed.

blocks.text: The selected icon is catalogued as a seventeenth- or eighteenth-century image of the Synaxis of the Three Holy Hierarchs. All three appear in episcopal vestments with Gospel books or scrolls. Their common presentation identifies this synaxis rather than an assembly of three unnamed bishops.

blocks.text: The OCA places the origin of their common observance in disputes among Christians at Constantinople who preferred one teacher over another. Its narrative recounts their appearance to John of Euchaita and the establishment of January 30 as a shared commemoration. The vision remains attributed to that ecclesiastical tradition.

blocks.text: The published account says the three reject factional rivalry and affirm their equality before God. Their combined icon accordingly belongs to a particular commemorated synaxis. It does not turn distinct biographies, writings, or historical settings into one anonymous author; readers can study the named teachers separately alongside the common image.
